talks.title: #15 No Privacy Left Outside Ziqi Zhang
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for #15 No Privacy Left Outside Ziqi Zhang.
talks.summary:
Overview: Ziqi Zhang presents at IEEE S&P on "No Privacy Left Outside," research examining the insecurity of TEE-based model deployment for on-device LLM protection.

Key Topics: LLMs as expensive sensitive assets requiring protection on edge devices; TEE deployment to prevent white-box model access; model stealing and membership inference attacks against TEE-protected models; and comparative evaluation of TEE partitioning schemes.

Technical Details: The research evaluates prior TEE-based defenses across model stealing and membership inference metrics, finding some schemes enable attacks 4.26x more effective than black-box baselines. Low-privileged database users can exploit partitioning weaknesses.

Takeaways: TEE-based LLM deployment provides insufficient protection against model stealing and membership inference. Model owners must evaluate defense effectiveness against realistic attack scenarios before trusting edge deployment.

talks.title: #144 TCP Spoofing Reliable Payload Transmission Past the Spoofed TCP Handshake Eric Pan
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #144 TCP Spoofing Reliable Payload Transmission Past the Spoofed TCP Handshake Eric Pan.
talks.summary:
TCP Spoofing Motivation

Eric Pan presents research on reliably transmitting payloads through spoofed TCP connections after handshake brute force. Attackers spoof victim IPs to bypass IP-based authentication in email SPF checks, database trust rules, and firewall allow lists.

Handshake Brute Force

Modern OSes hardened ISN prediction, pushing attackers toward brute-forcing sequence numbers with spoofed SYN and ACK floods. The harder problem is using the connection without knowing when it establishes or which sequence numbers are valid.

Send Window Brute Forcing

RFC acknowledgment rules permit old ACK values on new connections that acknowledge data never sent. Attackers split the search space into window-sized chunks, injecting payloads by brute-forcing acceptable ACK numbers on spoofed sessions.

Feedback Channels and Mitigation

A second primitive uses side channels—such as Linux SYN cookie ISN generation differences when listen backlogs fill—to confirm successful spoofing. Testing showed Windows, BSD, and Linux were vulnerable; Linux patched upstream and IETF work aims to tighten ACK validation.

talks.title: #498 Learn What You Want to Unlearn Unlearning Inversion Attacks against Machine Unlearning Hongsh
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for #498 Learn What You Want to Unlearn Unlearning Inversion Attacks against Machine Unlearning Hongsh.
talks.summary:
Machine Unlearning Basics

The speaker contrasts standard machine learning with machine unlearning, where specific training samples must be removed for reasons such as the right to be forgotten. Unlearning produces two model versions—the original and the unlearned model—which creates a new privacy attack surface beyond traditional membership inference.

Unlearning Inversion Attacks

The research asks whether confidential information within unlearned data can still be inferred. With white-box access to both models, attackers subtract parameters to recover gradient information and run optimization to invert features of removed samples. With black-box access, probing samples with balanced class confidence can reveal the unlearned label via the class whose confidence drops most.

Experimental Findings

Approximate unlearning leaks far more feature information than exact retraining-from-scratch unlearning, which benefits from training randomness. In multi-sample unlearning, full feature recovery is harder but partial inversion remains possible. Label inversion succeeds for both exact and approximate methods across single- and multi-class removal scenarios.

Defenses and Limitations

The team evaluated obfuscation, model pruning, and fine-tuning on additional data to blur differences between model pairs, but each defense caused unacceptable privacy-utility tradeoffs. They call for stronger post-unlearning protections against inversion attacks.

talks.title: #518 LACMUS Latent Concept Masking for General Robustness Enhancement of DNNs Hongsheng Hu
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #518 LACMUS Latent Concept Masking for General Robustness Enhancement of DNNs Hongsheng Hu.
talks.summary:
Robustness problem

Presenters from UNSW, Monash, and CSIRO at IEEE S&P introduce LACMUS (latent concept masking) to improve deep neural network robustness against adversarial pixel perturbations, semantic shifts such as lighting changes, and out-of-distribution samples where standard training fails.

Limits of adversarial training

Classic adversarial training mixes benign and adversarial examples but tends to be attack-specific, hurts clean accuracy, relies on low-level noise hard to interpret, and needs many adversarial samples. They identify four research gaps driving their method.

LACMUS approach

LACMUS encodes inputs through a VQ-VAE-style encoder into vectors matched against a pretrained concept codebook, masks or replaces concepts, decodes perturbed samples, and treats misclassified reconstructions as conceptual adversarial examples for training. Experiments using under one percent of training data report maintained clean accuracy and broader resilience to pixel, semantic, and distribution-shift attacks on MNIST and related sets.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Hongsheng Hu presents LACMUS (Latent Concept Masking for Robustness Enhancement), a framework designed to overcome the fundamental generalization limitations of adversarial training in deep neural networks (DNNs). Standard adversarial defenses typically overfit to specific pixel-level mathematical perturbations, compromising clean sample accuracy and failing to protect against semantic or distribution shifts. By utilizing a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) architecture to mask and perturb high-level concept vectors rather than individual pixels, LACMUS generates robust conceptual adversarial examples using less than 1% of standard training data.

Key Topics:
- The tri-fold vulnerability of deep neural networks: adversarial, semantic, and distribution robustness
- Four core research gaps in traditional adversarial training (attack-specific, variation-specific, utility tradeoff, low abstraction)
- Architecture of LACMUS: VQ-VAE encoders, pre-trained concept codebooks, and latent concept masking
- Empirical evaluation against FGSM, PGD, One-Pixel, spatial/hue transformations, and distribution drift

Technical Details:
Hu examines the three primary failure modes of modern deep neural networks: adversarial vulnerability (misclassification caused by imperceptible pixel noise), semantic vulnerability (failure under lighting, spatial, or environmental shifts), and distribution vulnerability (inability to handle out-of-distribution or corrupted data). While adversarial training is the standard defense, Hu identifies four critical limitations: it is attack-specific (defending against attack A fails against attack B), variation-specific (pixel-level noise training does not generalize to semantic rotations or lighting changes), suffers from a severe robustness-utility tradeoff (drastically reducing classification accuracy on clean, benign inputs), and operates at a low abstraction level that requires vast quantities of adversarial training data.

LACMUS addresses these deficiencies by operating within a latent conceptual space. The framework utilizes a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) comprising an encoder, a pre-trained concept codebook, and a decoder. The encoder maps a high-dimensional input image X into a grid of D-dimensional latent vectors V. These vectors are quantized against a discrete codebook C, where each codebook vector captures a distinct structural or semantic attribute of the class. LACMUS introduces a concept masking mechanism that systematically substitutes selected concept vectors (for example, swapping concept C9 with a baseline concept C0). The modified concept representation is fed into the VQ-VAE decoder to reconstruct a synthetic sample X'. If the reconstructed image induces misclassification while preserving the core visual structure, it is designated as a "conceptual adversarial example."

By augmenting model training with these conceptual adversarial examples, the DNN is compelled to base classification decisions on core invariant structures rather than superficial or non-essential features. In experimental evaluations, LACMUS utilized less than 1% of original training data samples while matching or improving clean baseline accuracy. Furthermore, models defended with LACMUS demonstrated broad generalization resilience, significantly outperforming standard adversarial training across gradient-based attacks (FGSM, PGD), pixel-budget attacks (One-Pixel), semantic transformations (spatial transformations, hue/lighting shifts), and challenging dataset corruptions (both hard in-distribution samples and out-of-distribution drift).

Key Takeaways:
Defenders training robust deep learning models should move away from brute-force pixel-level noise injection toward structured, concept-aware adversarial generation. Latent concept masking decouples defensive robustness from specific mathematical perturbation attacks, achieving generalized resistance across both adversarial noise and real-world semantic distortions. Furthermore, because concept masking operates on high-level representations, organizations can drastically reduce computational overhead and data requirements, training resilient models with minimal adversarial data budgets.

talks.title: 301 Scalable Verification of Zero Knowledge Protocols MIGUEL ISABEL MÁRQUEZ
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 301 Scalable Verification of Zero Knowledge Protocols MIGUEL ISABEL MÁRQUEZ.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Zero-knowledge (ZK) protocols allow a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing any secret information beyond the statement's validity. These protocols rely on completeness, soundness, and zero knowledge. Typically, statements are represented as arithmetic circuit satisfiability problems composed of addition and multiplication gates and encoded as quadratic constraint systems over large finite fields. A major source of vulnerabilities in ZK protocols is underconstrained bugs, where required constraints are omitted, enabling a malicious prover to produce verifiable proofs for invalid statements. This presentation introduces Cyber, a formal verification tool designed to automatically detect underconstrained bugs and verify Circom circuits against pre- and post-condition specifications.

### Key Topics
- **Zero-Knowledge Circuit Constraints**: Circuit representations in ZK systems strictly require quadratic constraints. In domain languages like Circom, developers work across symbolic constraint systems and executable witness generation code using different operators (`===`, `<--`, and `<==`). Improper combination can lead to circuits compiling successfully while generating empty or incomplete constraint systems.
- **Limitations of Existing Tools**: Existing verification techniques include syntactic checkers (Circom compiler inspect flag, Circomspect, Ecne) that only recognize standard surface patterns, and semantic tools (such as Picus) that suffer from scalability bottlenecks on large circuits and lack pre- and post-condition specification support.
- **Circom Tags**: Circom's type tagging mechanisms (e.g., specifying a binary signal tag) only enforce syntactic propagation checks during compilation rather than proving semantic satisfaction via actual constraints.

### Technical Details
Verification of ZK constraint systems faces two core challenges: reasoning over large finite fields involving nonlinear arithmetic operations, and scaling to circuits containing thousands to millions of constraints. Cyber overcomes these via two primary mechanisms:

1. **Transformation and Deduction Rules**: Standard SMT solvers (like Z3) frequently time out when handling nonlinear operations over finite fields. Cyber applies deduction and algebraic transformations to simplify operations before passing them to the solver. For example, quadratic equations like $a \cdot b = 0$ are rewritten into disjunctions ($a = 0 \lor b = 0$), and modulo operations are substituted with auxiliary variables ($k$) accompanied by computed tight bounds to constrain the search space.
2. **Modular Hierarchical Verification**: Instead of evaluating an entire flattened circuit containing millions of constraints simultaneously, Cyber leverages the circuit's hierarchical template structure. It verifies child components individually against their specifications, abstracts those subcomponents by replacing their internal constraint systems with their specification summaries, and uses those abstractions during parent component verification.

Formally, verification is cast as a satisfiability query: given circuit constraints $P$ and target specifications, the solver checks whether there exists an assignment that violates the specification (returning `sat` with a counterexample) or proves no violation is possible (`unsat`).

### Takeaways
Cyber was evaluated against widely used, real-world benchmarks, including production libraries such as `circomlib`, `zk-email`, and the `Dark Forest` game circuit codebase, as well as `B-Stark` (under development). Some evaluated circuits scaled up to 11 million constraints. Cyber verified most circuits with very few timeouts (which primarily occurred on complex mathematical structures such as elliptic curves). The tool identified previously undetected critical bugs, such as an underconstrained integer division bug in Dark Forest where the remainder was missing a constraint forcing it to be positive, allowing negative remainder counterexamples. Future work aims to extend Cyber to other ZK frameworks (Noir, Halo 2), alternative proving systems (Plonk), circuits defined solely as flat constraint systems, and extension fields.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, the speaker presents Pianist, a scalable, fully distributed zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocol designed for arbitrary arithmetic circuits, with applications targeting zkRollups and zkEVM on blockchains. While general-purpose schemes like Plonk provide quasi-linear proving time and constant proof size and verification time, scaling them on a single machine encounters severe bottlenecks in proof generation time and memory cost. Pianist addresses this challenge by distributing proof generation across a cluster while maintaining the asymptotic complexity of Plonk and requiring only constant communication between the master node and each worker node.

### Key Topics
- **Zero-Knowledge Proofs & zkRollups**: Leveraging succinct zero-knowledge proofs (such as Plonk) so untrusted parties can verify execution correctness without re-executing transactions, scaling blockchain systems.
- **Limitations of Prior Distributed ZKPs**: Earlier distributed systems such as DIZK (based on Groth16 and R1CS) and Z-Bridge (based on GKR and Virgo polynomial commitments) suffer from complex witness reductions or require linear communication.
- **Plonk Bottlenecks in Distributed Settings**: Distributed execution of the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) to compute witness polynomials normally requires inter-machine vector transpositions across butterfly networks, incurring linear communication overhead.
- **Pianist Architecture**: Bypassing cross-machine NTTs by partitioning circuits and using bivariate polynomial identities and distributed polynomial commitment schemes (PCS) like KZG.

### Technical Details
- **Bypassing Distributed NTT**: Rather than executing global butterfly transforms across machines, Pianist partitions the circuit into $M$ parts across $M$ machines and establishes an independent argument for each. Each vector holding distributed polynomials across machines is interpolated over powers of a root of unity to form a bivariate polynomial identity, which is verified on random challenge points via the Schwartz-Zippel lemma.
- **Interactive Protocol Execution**: Each worker node maintains its own polynomials and evaluates them at a challenge point $\alpha$ received from the verifier. Evaluations are transmitted to the master node, which constructs a new polynomial identity and commits to a witness ($H_y(\alpha, Y)$). The prover cluster then evaluates this on an additional random evaluation point from the verifier and produces a bivariate KZG opening proof.
- **Arbitrary Circuit Generalization & Robustness**: Pianist extends beyond data-parallel circuits to arbitrary arithmetic circuits by implementing a distributed grand product argument. Additionally, the master node can identify faulty proof fragments from worker nodes in data-parallel setups and generate proofs for correct slices without rerunning the entire cluster.
- **Implementation & Benchmarks**: Implemented on top of the Plonk codebase in the gnark library, Pianist demonstrates that proving time and memory usage scale down proportionally as cluster size grows, maintaining low overhead even with small numbers of worker nodes.

### Takeaways
Pianist offers a fully distributed ZKP protocol for general arithmetic circuits that preserves the constant proof size, constant verification time, and quasi-linear proving computation of Plonk while requiring only $O(1)$ constant communication between the master and worker nodes, effectively removing distributed communication bottlenecks in zkRollup scaling.
